title: When to Delegate a Decision
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This article challenges the popular image of the decisive, take-charge leader by arguing that the best leaders actually delegate as many decisions as possible rather than holding onto them. Retaining too many decisions creates a bottleneck that slows the whole team down, while teams accustomed to making their own calls become more engaged, more agile, and better prepared for future leadership roles. Delegation also frees leaders to focus their limited time on strategy and other work that genuinely requires their unique expertise. The one clear exception is strategy itself, which the author argues leaders must never hand off. The piece ends with a pointed line reframing any leader who feels overloaded with 'critical' decisions as likely fooling themselves about how many actually require their personal involvement.
points: Good leaders default to delegating decisions rather than retaining them
Leaders who hold too many decisions become bottlenecks that slow the whole team
Teams that regularly make their own decisions become more engaged, agile, and better prepared to lead
Strategy is the one category of decision leaders should never delegate
quotes: The truth is that good leaders do their best to push as many decisions as possible down to others on the team.
With any decision that needs to be made, they first ask who else can take it and make it.
Without empowering others to own as many decisions as possible, leaders soon become a bottleneck for getting things done.
In contrast, teams and team members who are used to making decisions feel trusted, are more engaged, and exhibit agility in the face of changes and challenges.
Leaders must never delegate strategy to others. But to accomplish that and still maintain the momentum of team progress, they must share decision-making on nearly everything else.
Any leader swamped with what they perceive to be a host of critical decisions that only they should or can make is usually fooling themselves.
